facts: Mary Shelley was 18 when she began writing "Frankenstein", and it was published anonymously in 1818 when she was 20.
The longest sentence in a classic novel is often cited from Victor Hugo's "Les Misérables": one sentence runs over 800 words.
Agatha Christie is the best-selling novelist of all time, with an estimated two billion copies sold across her works.
The word "nerd" first appeared in print in Dr. Seuss's 1950 book "If I Ran the Zoo".
Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote "The Gambler" in just 26 days to pay off a gambling debt, dictating it to a stenographer he later married.
"Don Quixote", published in two parts (1605 and 1615), is frequently called the first modern European novel.
A day on Venus is longer than its year: it takes 243 Earth days to rotate once but only 225 to orbit the Sun.
Neutron stars are so dense that a sugar-cube-sized amount of their material would weigh about a billion tonnes on Earth.
There is a giant cloud of alcohol in the constellation Aquila, roughly 1,000 times the diameter of our solar system.
The footprints left by Apollo astronauts on the Moon will likely last millions of years, since there is no wind or liquid water to erase them.
Saturn's density is so low that, given a large enough body of water, the planet would float.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth.
The term "artificial intelligence" was coined at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, widely regarded as the founding event of the field.
The perceptron, an early neural network, was built as a physical machine in 1958 and was expected by some to soon "walk, talk, see, and write".
ELIZA, a 1966 chatbot that mimicked a psychotherapist, fooled some users into believing it understood them, despite using simple pattern matching.
The "Turing Test", proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, was originally called the "Imitation Game".
AlphaGo's 2016 "move 37" against Lee Sedol was so unconventional that commentators initially thought it was a mistake.
Honey never spoils: sealed pots of honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs were still edible after thousands of years.
Searing meat does not "seal in" juices; that idea, popularized in the 1800s, has been repeatedly disproven, though searing does add flavor.
The Maillard reaction, responsible for browning and much of cooked food's flavor, was described by French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard in 1912.
Nutmeg is mildly hallucinogenic and toxic in large doses because it contains a compound called myristicin.
Carrots were originally purple and white; the familiar orange variety was cultivated in the Netherlands around the 16th–17th century.
The first speeding ticket was issued in 1896 to a driver going 8 mph in a 2 mph zone in Kent, England.
The Bugatti Veyron's tires cost tens of thousands of dollars per set and, at top speed, would drain a full tank of fuel in about 12 minutes.
Volkswagen means "people's car" in German; the Beetle became one of the best-selling car designs in history.
Cruise control was invented by Ralph Teetor, a mechanical engineer who was blind from childhood.
The average car spends roughly 95% of its lifetime parked.
Sunflowers exhibit heliotropism when young, turning to face the sun across the day, but mature flowers typically settle facing east.
Bananas are berries, botanically speaking, while strawberries are not.
Some bamboo species can grow up to nearly a metre in a single day under ideal conditions.
Marigolds are often planted alongside vegetables because their roots release compounds that can deter certain soil nematodes.
The world's oldest known living tree is a Great Basin bristlecone pine in California, estimated to be over 4,850 years old.
Russia spans 11 time zones, more than any other country on Earth.
The shortest scheduled commercial flight, between the Scottish islands of Westray and Papa Westray, lasts under two minutes.
Canada has the longest coastline of any country, at over 200,000 kilometres.
The Trans-Siberian Railway is the longest railway line in the world, running roughly 9,289 kilometres from Moscow to Vladivostok.
There is a single point where you can stand in four U.S. states at once: the Four Corners of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah.
